items.t: Pfizer's 5.9% Yield vs. AbbVie's 53-Year Dividend Streak: Which Stock Is the Better Buy?
sum: Pfizer (PFE +0.21%) and AbbVie (ABBV +0.20%) rank among the biggest drugmakers in the world. Both pharma stocks have also been favorites for many income investors through the years.

However, Pfizer and AbbVie offer distinctly different attractions for income investors these days. Pfizer's 5.9% dividend yield is one of the highest in the healthcare sector. AbbVie's 2.5% yield isn't as eye-catching, but the company has increased its dividend for an impressive 53 consecutive years. Which of these stocks is the better pick right now?

It's obvious what Pfizer's main argument is: the mouthwatering yield. An investor who bought $10,000 of Pfizer stock would receive nearly $600 per year, compared to only around $250 from investing the same amount in AbbVie.

But is Pfizer's dividend safe? The company's payout ratio of roughly 246% could alarm some investors. However, that ratio is based on Pfizer's GAAP earnings, which include some one-time items such as acquisition-related costs that muddy the waters.

A better metric for assessing Pfizer's dividend safety is its free cash flow payout ratio. That number currently stands at 89%. Granted, Pfizer doesn't have much wiggle room at this level, but it's much more reassuring than the GAAP earnings-based payout ratio.

Importantly, Pfizer's management is adamant that no dividend cuts are forthcoming despite the company facing a patent cliff over the next couple of years. CFO Cecile Guegan said in the company's third-quarter earnings call, "So through the LOE [loss of exclusivity] period, our operating cash flow, financial assets, and access to capital markets will give us the ability to continue to invest and maintain the dividend."

The patent cliff will negatively impact Pfizer's revenue and earnings growth, though. Still, the company thinks that its newer products and late-stage pipeline candidates will help it return to growth later this decade.

AbbVie stock in focus after positive QULIPTA migraine trial
sum: AbbVie is gaining a fresh pipeline catalyst after positive Phase 3 results for QULIPTA in migraine prevention. A Yahoo Finance report published Thursday, November 12, said the TEMPLE study produced favorable results for atogepant, marketed as QULIPTA, in a head-to-head comparison with topiramate.

The 24-week blinded phase compared the two oral treatments in adults with migraine. According to the report, 12 percent of patients receiving atogepant stopped treatment because of side effects, compared with 30 percent of those taking topiramate. The study also showed better efficacy for QULIPTA on key migraine-prevention endpoints.

The readout strengthens AbbVie's position in oral migraine prevention, where treatment persistence is commercially important. Better tolerability can support continued use, while stronger prevention results may improve the product's competitive profile. The trial outcome alone, however, does not establish future prescription growth or revenue.

AbbVie is using immunology and neuroscience to support growth as older products face increasing competition, the Yahoo Finance analysis said. The report highlighted QULIPTA alongside Ubrelvy as part of the company's migraine franchise and pointed to future quarterly disclosures as the next opportunity to assess commercial traction.

Is AbbVie Stock Really Expensive?
sum: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

AbbVie (ABBV) stock trades at 50.4 times its earnings over the past twelve months, compared with 21.9 times for the S&P 500. Anyone buying at that multiple is paying now for profit AbbVie has yet to report, and the business has to grow into its price. So how fast would AbbVie have to grow just for today’s share price to hold?

At its current price, AbbVie would need to grow revenue about 16.6% a year for five years merely to maintain its share price, offering no return on top. Over the four quarters ended September 30, 2026, its revenue grew 10.7%. The years, the mature P/E and the steady net margin are Trefis assumptions.

AbbVie’s market value was $521 billion at the November 12, 2026 close. At a mature P/E of 22.8, that value would mean annual net income of $22.8 billion. At a steady net margin of 16.1%, that profit would take revenue of $142 billion by fiscal Q3 2031. That margin is just above AbbVie’s best twelve-month net margin of 15.7% over the last twelve quarter-ends, and well above the 8.5% average over that span. The revenue needed is more than double the $66.0 billion AbbVie reported over the past twelve months. Trefis allows five years because today’s P/E is more than twice the mature one.

Trefis built the mature P/E mostly from the 18.0 level it uses for pharmaceuticals and biotechnology companies, with a 40% weight on AbbVie’s own average. That average was 81.0 over the last twelve quarter-ends. Trefis caps any company average above 30 at 30, so AbbVie’s average counts only as 30.

Not so far. Management expects revenue of about $67.8 billion for fiscal 2026, against the $61.2 billion AbbVie reported for fiscal 2025, it said on the October 30, 2026 call. That is growth of about 10.8%, near today’s pace, and only fiscal Q4 2026, the last quarter of that guided year, falls inside the five years. Management will give 2027 guidance on its fourth-quarter call.

The immunology drugs Skyrizi and Rinvoq are the two largest drugs in the guidance. Skyrizi sold $17.6 billion in fiscal 2025, and management expects $21.8 billion for fiscal 2026; Rinvoq sold $8.3 billion in fiscal 2025, and management expects $10.3 billion for fiscal 2026.

Could AbbVie Stock Survive A Skyrizi And Rinvoq Slowdown?
sum: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

Skyrizi and Rinvoq are AbbVie’s (ABBV) two biggest drugs, and a slowdown in them is the risk a holder should weigh. Together they made up about 42% of AbbVie’s revenue in 2025. The worry is not idle: on its October 30, 2026 call, management said the pair has been on the market for 8 years and faces more competition, though it made that point to stress that both are still growing fast. The same day, AbbVie reported revenue that rose on strength in immunology and neuroscience. So has that competition started to slow either drug?
Not in the latest quarter. In fiscal Q3 2026, Skyrizi sales reached nearly $5.8 billion, up 22.9% on an operational basis. Rinvoq grew faster still, posting sales of $2.7 billion, up 24.3%.

Management said recent oral competition is not having a substantive impact on Skyrizi in psoriasis, where the drug still wins roughly 1 out of every 2 new or switching patients. AbbVie also raised its full-year Skyrizi sales guidance for the third time in 2026.

AbbVie has seen what happens when competition does take hold. Humira sales were $683 million in the quarter, down 30.6% on an operational basis, which management put down to continued competition from biosimilars, close copies of the drug.

Management expects about $67.8 billion of revenue for 2026, compared with the $61.2 billion reported for 2025. Of that $6.6 billion rise, management says Skyrizi and Rinvoq are adding $6 billion. Vraylar is growing too, but shrinking sales for Humira and Imbruvica leave the two biggest drugs to generate most of the net gain.

A slowdown in the two drugs would therefore show up first as slower revenue growth for AbbVie, not as lower total sales. That growth matters for the price you pay: AbbVie stock trades at 7.9 times its sales, against 3.2 for the S&P 500, which suggests buyers are paying for growth.

Is AbbVie (NYSE:ABBV) Beyond the Humira Cliff?
sum: - As biosimilar rivals chipped away at Humira, the company redirected its commercial muscle toward Skyrizi and Rinvoq, widening their approved uses across skin, joint and bowel conditions.
- At a recent gastroenterology congress, the company presented fresh data across inflammatory bowel disease, spanning Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis.
- Immunology has matured into among the largest arenas in medicine, spanning dermatology, rheumatology and gastroenterology, with makers racing to widen uses and sharpen dosing.

The story is notable because Humira was for years among the best-selling medicines ever, and its decline of patent protection posed a daunting test. By building successors before the cliff arrived, the company engineered a handoff that has so far held, keeping immunology at the heart of its identity. The smoothness of the handoff has become a reference point across the drug world for how a maker can navigate a historic patent cliff. AbbVie (NYSE:ABBV) Healthcare AbbVie Inc (NYSE:ABBV) 294.38 USD +1.080 0.368% Last Updated at: 2026-11-10T20:54:00Z is part of the S&P 500, Russell 1000 and NYSE Composite.

Beyond today's growth drivers, the company has worked to stock a deeper bench, advancing combination regimens for bowel disease and next-generation antibodies aimed at skin conditions. Programs pairing its medicines with novel mechanisms seek to push remission rates higher in hard-to-treat patients. Dealmaking has supplemented internal research, bringing in long-acting antibodies and other platforms meant to extend the franchise into the next decade. Widening the pipeline is central to the plan, since even well-performing medicines eventually face their own competition and patent timelines. Combination regimens and next-generation antibodies form the heart of the company's plan to extend its lead, pushing remission rates higher in patients who respond poorly to current options. Supplementing internal research with acquired platforms gives the maker several paths to keep the franchise growing into the next decade.
Humira revenue has fallen sharply as biosimilars spread across the American market, a decline the company anticipated and prepared for.

AbbVie stock adds Nxera IBD candidate to immunology pipeline
sum: AbbVie expanded its immunology pipeline on Wednesday, November 4, by taking exclusive worldwide rights to Nxera Pharma's investigational NXE0033744 for inflammatory bowel disease. The terms were announced in a Nxera Pharma release.

NXE0033744 is an oral EP4 receptor agonist designed to act locally in the gastrointestinal tract. Nxera said its completed Phase 1 program supported a gut-selective profile and target engagement. The candidate is not approved, so additional clinical evidence and regulatory decisions will determine whether the program can progress.

Nxera will receive USD 100 million upfront and is eligible for up to USD 1.37 billion in development and commercial milestone payments, plus tiered royalties on net sales. The transaction remains subject to customary antitrust clearances, including review under the Hart-Scott-Rodino Act.

The agreement adds another potential immunology asset as AbbVie develops its portfolio beyond established products. The next material signals are the timing and design of further clinical work, efficacy data in inflammatory bowel disease and any regulatory filing.

sum: AbbVie strengthened its investment case during the week ended Saturday, November 7, with stronger third-quarter results, a higher full-year outlook and two pipeline developments. The company reported the results on October 30, covering the quarter ended September 30, 2026.

According to AbbVie, third-quarter revenue rose 10.3 percent year over year to 17.4 billion US dollars. Adjusted earnings reached 3.82 US dollars per share. AbbVie lifted its 2026 adjusted diluted earnings guidance to 13.95 to 13.99 US dollars per share from 13.76 to 13.96 US dollars and raised its revenue outlook by 200 million US dollars to 67.8 billion US dollars.

The outlook includes an unfavorable 0.69 US dollar per-share impact from acquired in-process research and development and milestone expenses incurred through the third quarter. AbbVie said the guidance excludes similar expenses that may arise after the quarter.

AbbVie also signed an exclusive global license with Nxera for NXE0033744, an investigational EP4 receptor agonist for inflammatory bowel disease. The agreement includes a 100 million US dollar upfront payment and up to 1.37 billion US dollars in development and commercial milestones, plus tiered royalties. The transaction remains subject to customary antitrust clearances, according to Pharmaceutical Executive.

Separately, AbbVie expanded its Oxford research facility in the United Kingdom. The new 12,000-square-foot site supports research in immunology, neuroscience and oncology and forms part of more than 120 million pounds invested and committed across the UK life-sciences ecosystem, the company said in its Oxford announcement.

AbbVie Stock Hits a Record After a 5.2% Dividend Raise: Why Its 276% Payout Ratio Doesn’t Tell the Entire Story
sum: - AbbVie raised 2026 adjusted EPS guidance to $13.95 to $13.99 and lifted its quarterly dividend 5.2% to $1.82, as Skyrizi and Rinvoq sales each grew more than 22%.
- The GAAP payout ratio of 275.84% overstates the strain: the new $7.28 annual dividend uses about 52% of adjusted earnings, and Street estimates put that near 40% by 2028.
- The stock’s run to a record $294.89 has cut the forward yield to about 2.47%, which puts the focus on 2027 guidance at the fourth-quarter call.

AbbVie (ABBV) gave dividend investors the answer they were waiting for on Friday, October 30. Its third-quarter report showed revenue of $17.404 billion, up 10.3%, and adjusted EPS of $3.82. It also raised full-year adjusted EPS guidance to $13.95 to $13.99, from $13.76 to $13.96, and lifted the quarterly dividend 5.2% to $1.82 a share, starting with the February 16, 2027 payment.

Skyrizi and Rinvoq did the heavy lifting again. Skyrizi sales rose 22.7% to $5.776 billion and Rinvoq rose 23.9% to $2.706 billion, and on the earnings call management lifted their full-year targets to $21.8 billion and $10.3 billion. The stock closed at a record $294.89, up 1.4%.

In September, AbbVie stock’s 2.74% yield sat near a two-year low while its payout ratio looked stretched. The open question was simple: could earnings grow fast enough to fund another raise without the payout climbing further?

Friday’s numbers say yes. The headline doubling in Q3 adjusted EPS, from $1.86, is mostly a base effect: last year’s quarter carried a $1.50 charge for acquired R&D, against $0.11 this time. Strip that out of both quarters and adjusted EPS still rose about 17%, from $3.36 to $3.93. A 5.2% dividend increase is a small slice of that.

A central feature of the company's agreement is the direct-to-consumer channel through which patients can obtain certain medicines at discounted cash prices. The arrangement extends to select immunology, ophthalmology, and metabolic treatments, offering cash-pay patients a more direct route to the medicines than the traditional system has allowed. For the company, the channel offers a way to serve patients who lack generous coverage, a group that has often struggled to afford branded medicines at their list prices. The primary catalyst driving the upward momentum and intraday volatility in AbbVie's stock is a sweeping regulatory development impacting the broader pharmaceutical sector. The Trump administration has proposed a new rule to modify reimbursement rates under the 340B Drug Pricing Program, aiming to curb hospital markups on outpatient medications. By capping how much hospitals can charge for discounted drugs, the policy shifts financial margins back in favor of major drug developers and away from hospital intermediaries. This policy alters the structural dynamics of the drug distribution market, igniting a strong rally across major pharmaceutical names and propelling AbbVie to a new 52-week high as investors anticipate enhanced margin retention for manufacturers.

Adding to this positive momentum is the highly favorable market reception to AbbVie's strategic acquisition of Apogee Therapeutics. Analysts view the acquisition as a pivotal defensive expansion of AbbVie’s already dominant immunology franchise. By securing Apogee's promising clinical-stage pipeline, particularly in atopic dermatitis and asthma, the company is effectively building a secondary moat to sustain long-term revenue growth. This proactive portfolio diversification provides an attractive hedge against future patent expirations of legacy blockbusters.

Operational and pipeline execution have further bolstered investor confidence. AbbVie focuses on high-margin specialty medicines in immunology and oncology, while Pfizer operates a broader portfolio spanning vaccines, primary care, and specialized cancer treatments. sum: AbbVie (ABBV +1.06%), a pharmaceutical giant, is set to release its first-quarter earnings report on April 29. The stock has not performed well so far this year, with shares down 13% as of writing. Could the drugmaker's quarterly update be the catalyst that helps it recover? Let's find out whether it's worth it to invest in AbbVie before its next earnings report.

AbbVie is entering its quarterly update with solid momentum for its key growth pillars, Skyrizi and Rinvoq. These two immunology medicines have replaced Humira, once the world's best-selling drug, whose revenue peaked at $21.2 billion. The pharmaceutical leader is projecting that Skyrizi and Rinvoq will cross $31 billion in combined annual sales in 2026, one year ahead of schedule. The market will expect strong first-quarter performances for both.

On the other hand, one possible worry might be that other growth drivers aren't pulling their weight. AbbVie's Humira, which lost patent exclusivity in the U.S. in 2023, remained its third best-selling therapy last year. That should change in the first quarter if other franchises perform well while Humira's descent into eventual irrelevance continues. But if Humira maintains its spot, the market could punish AbbVie if it sees weakness in other growth franchises as the reason.

Another possible problem lies with AbbVie's cancer medicine Imbruvica, whose sales have been declining due to competition. It is now the subject of government price negotiations that should lead to even lower revenue. Provided AbbVie can post solid growth despite that -- perhaps matching or even exceeding its $14.7 billion projected net revenue for the period, implying year-over year growth of about 10% -- the company's share might soar.

Of course, that will depend on other factors as well, including AbbVie's outlook for the rest of the year and potential clinical or regulatory developments. So, is AbbVie stock a buy before its earnings release? My view is that it depends on what each investor is looking for. It's always challenging to predict how the market will react even to solid quarterly updates -- so AbbVie's shares could move one way or the other (or barely show any movement) on April 29.

Skyrizi and Rinvoq delivered combined 2025 revenues of approximately $25.9 billion, up more than $8 billion year-over-year, already surpassing AbbVie’s own 2027 combined guidance by $500 million and capturing roughly 75% of new frontline IBD patient starts.

Chief Commercial Officer Jeffrey Stewart stated on the Q4 2025 earnings call that “Skyrizi and Rinvoq are a great pair in IBD…together, our two brands have already exceeded peak Humira sales by more than $4.5 billion and are on pace to deliver more than 20% growth in 2026,” anchoring investor confidence heading into the subcutaneous label expansion.

AbbVie’s $21.5 billion Skyrizi guide, $10.1 billion Rinvoq guide, and a confirmed Parkinson’s franchise targeting more than $5 billion in peak sales position the company for high single-digit revenue growth through 2029, with $18.5 billion in free cash flow expected this year alone.

The AFFIRM data confirming Skyrizi’s subcutaneous Crohn’s induction works directly extends the drug’s frontline dominance into a more patient-friendly format, removing the IV administration barrier that still limits biologic penetration in IBD.

sum: AbbVie ABBV stock slipped below its 50-day simple moving average (SMA) on March 13, after consistently trading above it since mid-Feb. However, the stock has remained comfortably above its 200-day SMA for more than six months.

When a stock slips below the 50-day SMA, it indicates an intermediate correction that could be due to lack of news flow . With the stock staying above the 200-day SMA, its long-term uptrend is still intact as its fundamentals are strong.

Such a scenario can confuse investors about whether to buy the dip, exit the stock, or hold it based on long-term trends. Let's examine the company's strengths and weaknesses to better analyze how to play AbbVie stock in this situation.

AbbVie lost patent protection for its blockbuster drug, Humira, in the United States in January 2023 and in the EU in 2018. Humira's sales are declining due to loss of exclusivity (LOE) and biosimilar erosion. AbbVie has successfully navigated the LOE of Humira, a drug that once generated more than 50% of its total revenues. It has accomplished this by launching two other successful new immunology medicines, Skyrizi and Rinvoq, which are performing extremely well, bolstered by approvals in new indications, and should support top-line growth in the next few years.

Skyrizi and Rinvoq generated combined sales of $26.0 billion in 2025, exceeding expectations and representing year-over-year growth of more than 40%. The drugs delivered strong performance across all approved indications, especially in the popular inflammatory bowel disease space, which includes two conditions — ulcerative colitis (UC) and Crohn's disease. In 2026, AbbVie expects combined Skyrizi and Rinvoq sales of more than $31 billion.

Strong immunology market growth, market share gains and momentum from new indications, as well as the potential for five new indications for Rinvoq over the next few years, are expected to drive the drugs' growth. Rinvoq could be approved for two indications — vitiligo and alopecia areata — in 2026. Phase III data on Rinvoq in hidradenitis suppurativa and systemic lupus erythematosus are expected this year. AbbVie believes that the next wave of potential approvals in Rinvoq could add roughly $2 billion to peak-year sales for the product.

Where Will AbbVie Be in 5 Years?
sum: A lot has changed for AbbVie (ABBV +0.68%) over the past five years. Notably, the biotech company's Humira, once its biggest growth driver and the world's best-selling drug, lost patent exclusivity in the U.S. in 2023. Despite that setback, AbbVie has produced solid returns over the last half a decade.
But can the drugmaker maintain that momentum through 2031? Let's find out how things might unfold for AbbVie over the next five years.

AbbVie has performed relatively well despite the Humira patent cliff, thanks to two other immunology medicines: Skyrizi and Rinvoq. These products should drive solid top-line growth through the end of the decade and beyond. Neither will lose patent protection by 2031, and thanks to their approvals across several inflammatory diseases and potential label expansions, their medium-term prospects look bright.

Rinvoq, for instance, could soon earn new indications in treating alopecia areata and vitiligo, new markets that will help boost its sales. Beyond these two main growth drivers, though, AbbVie could also make meaningful progress with newer approvals and late-stage pipeline candidates. Last year, the company received approval to market Emrelis, a medicine for non-small cell lung cancer.

That aligns with the company's strategy to aggressively expand in oncology (it has historically dominated in immunology). And it boasts several other candidates that could earn approval in the next five years. One of them, ABBV-400, is currently undergoing phase 3 studies in colorectal cancer.

AbbVie's pipeline features candidates across other therapeutic areas, including neuroscience and eye care. The company even entered into a licensing agreement to develop a weight loss medicine. By 2031, AbbVie's portfolio of approved drugs should look more diversified, although its immunology lineup will still be the main growth franchise. And importantly, the company does not expect a major loss of patent exclusivity through the end of the decade.

AbbVie will face some challenges through 2031. For instance, the company's cancer drug Imbruvica was targeted by the government for price negotiation -- negotiated prices kicked in this year. The good news is that Imbruvica's sales were already declining and no longer featured prominently in AbbVie's growth plans.

AbbVie, hitting record sales on Skyrizi gains, holds its own in growing IBD arena despite J&J competition
sum: Billions of dollars in U.S. biosimilar erosion to AbbVie’s blockbuster immunology drug Humira is no match for its rising superstar Skyrizi. Despite the fall of what was once the world’s top-selling drug, one thing is certain: AbbVie’s immunology portfolio is still on top.
In the two years since Humira first faced biosimilar competition, AbbVie’s newer Skyrizi and Rinvoq have more than picked up the slack.

In 2025, the duo propelled the company to a record-breaking $61.1 billion in total sales, an 8.6% increase over 2024 that eclipsed the company’s previous peak revenue of $58 billion in 2022. The new landmark was reached despite nearly $16 billion of U.S. Humira erosion that has set in since then, CEO Robert Michael said on AbbVie’s fourth-quarter and full-year earnings conference call.

Together, Skyrizi, Rinvoq and Humira made up $30.4 billion of those sales, representing 14% year-over-year growth. Although Humira sales dissipated to $4.5 billion over the year, Skyrizi pulled far ahead to $17.5 billion, while Rinvoq is chugging along with $8.3 billion in yearly sales.
The trio helped the company surpass its initial 2025 guidance by more than $2 billion, Michael pointed out.

One of the biggest growth drivers of sales for both Skyrizi and Rinvoq is the inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) market, an umbrella term that constitutes both Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis. Skyrizi specifically holds an in-play capture rate of 75% among IL-23 drugs in the frontline IBD setting, chief commercial officer Jeffrey Stewart said, touting a “strong and consistent” share performance even as the IL-23 drug class “grows rapidly.”

One such IL-23 that makes formidable competition for the immunology duo across the same indications is Johnson & Johnson’s Tremfya. The drug, which J&J positioned to take on sales from older Stelara à la AbbVie’s Humira strategy, rounded out its IBD uses with a Crohn’s disease nod early last year, solidifying its competitive label in the IBD market.

2 Healthcare Dividend Stocks That are Just What the Doctor Ordered
sum: Healthcare stocks are not known for healthy dividends. Great for growth, yes, but often so-so for dividend yields. The average medical large-cap stock's dividend yield was 1.67% at the end of 2025, sixth among the 11 sectors for large-cap stocks.

Unlike utilities, which can rely on steady, fixed revenue sources, healthcare companies must continually invest in research and development (R&D). That's because sales for blockbuster drugs made by pharmaceutical companies decline when their patents expire and they face generic competition. Research and development is also important for medical equipment stocks, so often the priority is on funding new products rather than returning dividends to shareholders.

However, there are healthcare stocks that have consistently grown their dividend, and whose yields are above-average, and these companies have the free cash flow needed to keep growing their dividends. AbbVie (ABBV +0.02%) and Medtronic (MDT -1.81%) are two such stocks.
AbbVie: Dividend giant among large-cap pharmaceutical companies

AbbVie has a dividend yield of 2.98%. The company has been around only since it was spun off from Abbott Laboratories (ABT -1.36%) in 2013, but including its time as a part of Abbott, it has increased its quarterly dividend for 54 consecutive years. That makes it a Dividend King, one of only 56 companies that have increased their dividends for 50 or more years. AbbVie has already raised its dividend by 5.5% this year to $1.73 per share.

In the third quarter, the pharma giant reported revenue of $15.8 billion, up 9% year over year. Earnings per share (EPS) were $1.86, a 38% decline from the same quarter in 2024, driven by increased spending on in-process research and development and milestone expenses.

The company has successfully transitioned from replacing Humira, once the world's top-selling drug, to a wider portfolio that includes two other immunology blockbuster therapies, Rinvoq and Skyrizi. A decade ago, Humira brought in 63% of the company's revenue. In the most recent quarter, Skyrizi was the company's top-selling drug with $4.7 billion in the quarter, with Rinvoq bringing in $2.2 billion in sales and Humira bringing in $993 million.

sum: AbbVie (NYSE:ABBV) told investors on Wednesday that its fourth-quarter earnings could be affected by charges linked to acquired in-process research and development and milestone expenses, pointing to continued financial implications from recent deal activity. In a regulatory filing, the company disclosed a $1.3 billion pre-tax charge that is expected to weigh on both GAAP and adjusted earnings per share, adding to near-term earnings pressure tied to acquisitions.

Revolution Medicines stock surges over 20% on potential AbbVie acquisition
sum: Investing.com -- Revolution Medicines (NASDAQ:RVMD) stock surged 29% before trading was halted twice due to volatility following a Wall Street Journal report that AbbVie (NYSE:ABBV) is in advanced talks to acquire the clinical-stage precision oncology company.

According to people familiar with the matter, AbbVie is nearing a deal that could value Revolution Medicines at approximately $20 billion or more, representing a premium to the company's current market value of around $16 billion. The acquisition could be finalized soon, barring any last-minute complications.

The news triggered significant gains across the oncology biotech sector, with several of Revolution's peers seeing substantial price movements. Verastem (NASDAQ:VSTM) jumped 25%, while Tango Therapeutics (NASDAQ:TNGX) climbed 20%, and Erasca (NASDAQ:ERAS) soared 27%.

Revolution Medicines specializes in developing novel targeted therapies for RAS-addicted cancers. The potential acquisition could strengthen AbbVie's oncology portfolio as it seeks to expand its presence in the precision medicine space.

The companies have not officially confirmed the talks, and it remains unclear exactly how much AbbVie is offering for the biotech firm. Trading in Revolution Medicines shares was halted following the rapid price increase triggered by the report.
